title: Graph algorithms
summary: Shortest paths, MSTs, and topo order — pick by weights and cycles.

parts.rule: Map the ask to a standard engine: BFS when every edge weighs one; Dijkstra when weights are non-negative; Bellman-Ford when negatives exist (and to flag negative cycles); single-pass relaxation in topological order on DAGs; Kruskal or Prim for undirected MSTs. Speak the weight and direction assumptions before naming the algorithm. Selection is the skill; coding the heap is secondary.
parts.why: People reach for Dijkstra on every shortest-path prompt, including negative edges, or run dense all-pairs methods on sparse single-source cases. Interviewers score the selection more than the heap details. Naming assumptions (no negatives, undirected, acyclic) is the real skill on display.
parts.example: Undirected weighted edges: 1-2 cost 4, 1-3 cost 1, 3-2 cost 1, 2-4 cost 3. Dijkstra from 1 sets dist[1]=0, first takes 1→3 (distance 1), then 3→2 (distance 2), then 2→4 (distance 5). Path 1-3-2 beats the direct 1-2 edge of cost 4. Plain BFS would treat every edge as weight 1 and claim distance 1 to node 2. For an MST with Kruskal, sort edges (1-3:1, 3-2:1, 2-4:3, 1-2:4); add 1-3, add 3-2, add 2-4; skip 1-2 because both ends already share a component. MST total weight is 5. On a course DAG with hour-weighted edges, topological order then one relaxation pass yields single-source longest or shortest paths in linear time over nodes plus edges.
parts.use: Use BFS for unit-weight shortest hops. Use Dijkstra with a min-heap for non-negative weights. Use Bellman-Ford for negatives or negative-cycle detection. Use Kruskal or Prim for undirected MSTs. Use topo plus relaxation on DAGs when a cycle is impossible by construction.
parts.refuse: Do not run Dijkstra when negative edges exist. Do not apply undirected MST algorithms to directed graphs. Do not pick dense all-pairs Floyd for a single-source sparse query without need. Do not claim a topological order while a cycle remains.

body:
Rule. Map the ask to a standard engine: BFS when every edge weighs one; Dijkstra when weights are non-negative; Bellman-Ford when negatives exist (and to flag negative cycles); single-pass relaxation in topological order on DAGs; Kruskal or Prim for undirected MSTs. Speak the weight and direction assumptions before naming the algorithm. Selection is the skill; coding the heap is secondary.

Why it matters. People reach for Dijkstra on every shortest-path prompt, including negative edges, or run dense all-pairs methods on sparse single-source cases. Interviewers score the selection more than the heap details. Naming assumptions (no negatives, undirected, acyclic) is the real skill on display.

Worked example. Undirected weighted edges: 1-2 cost 4, 1-3 cost 1, 3-2 cost 1, 2-4 cost 3. Dijkstra from 1 sets dist[1]=0, first takes 1→3 (distance 1), then 3→2 (distance 2), then 2→4 (distance 5). Path 1-3-2 beats the direct 1-2 edge of cost 4. Plain BFS would treat every edge as weight 1 and claim distance 1 to node 2. For an MST with Kruskal, sort edges (1-3:1, 3-2:1, 2-4:3, 1-2:4); add 1-3, add 3-2, add 2-4; skip 1-2 because both ends already share a component. MST total weight is 5. On a course DAG with hour-weighted edges, topological order then one relaxation pass yields single-source longest or shortest paths in linear time over nodes plus edges.

When to use. Use BFS for unit-weight shortest hops. Use Dijkstra with a min-heap for non-negative weights. Use Bellman-Ford for negatives or negative-cycle detection. Use Kruskal or Prim for undirected MSTs. Use topo plus relaxation on DAGs when a cycle is impossible by construction.

When to refuse. Do not run Dijkstra when negative edges exist. Do not apply undirected MST algorithms to directed graphs. Do not pick dense all-pairs Floyd for a single-source sparse query without need. Do not claim a topological order while a cycle remains.
